summary.en: A highly contagious viral disease causing fever, mouth and foot blisters, and severe production losses in cloven-hoofed animals.
summary.ku: نەخۆشییەکی ڤایرۆسی زۆر گوازرەوەیە کە تا، پەپولەی دەم و پێ و کەمبوونی بەرهەم دروست دەکات لە ئاژەڵانی لکپێ.
summary.ar: مرض فيروسي شديد العدوى يسبب الحمى وتقرحات الفم والقدمين وخسائر إنتاجية كبيرة في الحيوانات مشقوقة الظلف.

diseases.zoonoticNote: Not considered a practical public-health zoonosis. Human infection is very rare; normal hygiene and PPE are still advised.
diseases.notifiableNote: Foot-and-mouth disease is a WOAH-listed disease and is reportable in most countries. Report any suspicion immediately and do not move animals.
diseases.meatNote: Carcasses of affected or suspect animals are condemned under official outbreak regulations; meat must not enter the food chain.
diseases.causativeAgent: Foot-and-mouth disease virus (Aphthovirus, family Picornaviridae), with multiple serotypes. It is very stable in cool, damp conditions and spreads by direct contact, contaminated people, vehicles and animal products.
diseases.affected: Cattle, sheep, goats, pigs and other cloven-hoofed animals. All ages can be affected; young calves may die suddenly.
symptoms: High fever, often 40–41°C, with dullness and a sudden milk drop
Blisters and raw erosions on the tongue, gums, lips and muzzle
Profuse drooling, lip smacking and reluctance to eat
Blisters between the claws and on the coronary band; marked lameness
Teat lesions and painful milking
Sudden death in young calves due to heart damage
diseases.diagnosis: Clinical signs are strongly suggestive. Confirm through official channels by RT-PCR or virus detection on vesicular fluid or epithelium, and paired serology where appropriate. Do not collect samples without advice from the veterinary authority.
diseases.postMortem: Vesicles and erosions in the mouth, tongue, dental pad, teats and coronary bands, often ruptured by the time of death. Calves may show pale streaky myocardial necrosis (tiger heart). Rumen and abomasal erosions can occur. Do not open a suspect carcass without official advice; submit vesicular epithelium and fluid through the official channel.
diseases.treatment: There is no specific antiviral treatment. Provide soft feed and water, wound care, anti-inflammatory support if advised, and antibiotics only for secondary bacterial infection under veterinary direction. National outbreak policy may require culling and movement controls.
diseases.prevention: Use strain-matched vaccination where officially permitted, with strict biosecurity, quarantine, movement control and disinfection. Do not vaccinate in an outbreak without official instruction. Report suspicion at once.

summary.en: Inflammation of the udder, usually caused by bacteria entering the teat canal. It reduces milk quality and is a major welfare and economic problem.
summary.ku: هەوکردنی مەمک، زۆرجار بەهۆی باکتریاکان کە لە کۆتایی سرەتەوە دەچنە ژوورەوە. کوالیتی شیر کەم دەکات و کێشەیەکی گەورەی ئابووری و ئاژەڵییە.
summary.ar: التهاب الضرع، وغالباً تسببه بكتيريا تدخل عبر قناة الحلمة. يقلل جودة الحليب ويشكل مشكلة اقتصادية ورفاهية مهمة.

diseases.zoonoticNote: Not generally regarded as a zoonosis, but milk from affected cows can carry dangerous bacteria and drug residues. Never sell milk outside withdrawal rules.
diseases.notifiableNote: Not usually notifiable, although specific pathogens and local rules can differ.
diseases.meatNote: Meat from recovered animals may enter the food chain after official slaughter inspection and full observance of antibiotic withdrawal periods.
diseases.causativeAgent: Usually bacteria: Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus uberis, S. dysgalactiae, Escherichia coli, Klebsiella and others. Contagious pathogens spread during milking; environmental pathogens come from bedding and manure.
diseases.affected: Lactating and dry dairy cows, especially high-yielding cows and those in early lactation. Heifers and beef cows can also be affected.
symptoms: A hot, painful, swollen quarter or quarters
Clots, flakes, watery or discoloured milk
A sudden fall in milk yield
Fever, dullness and reduced appetite in acute cases
Cold, dark or gangrenous udder tissue, collapse or sepsis in severe toxic cases
diseases.diagnosis: Inspect and strip all four quarters. Use the California Mastitis Test and submit a milk sample for culture and sensitivity where needed. Herd somatic cell counts help detect subclinical mastitis. Severe cases require a full physical examination.
diseases.postMortem: The affected quarter is swollen, firm and may contain clotted, watery or blood-stained milk; abscesses and gangrene occur in severe cases. The supramammary lymph node may be enlarged. In peracute coliform mastitis the gland is oedematous and congested. Culture of milk or tissue identifies the pathogen, because gross lesions alone do not.
diseases.treatment: Milk out the affected quarter frequently and provide supportive care. Use intramammary or systemic antibiotics only when indicated, following culture results and national withdrawal rules. NSAIDs may help pain and inflammation. Toxic mastitis is an emergency.
diseases.prevention: Use clean dry bedding, good milking hygiene, post-milking teat disinfection, correctly maintained milking machines and regular teat scoring. Consider internal teat sealants and dry-cow therapy where appropriate. Control flies and cull chronic high-cell-count cows.

summary.en: A chronic bacterial infection that causes late-term abortion, infertility and swollen joints. It is an important zoonosis and a major herd-health and trade issue.
summary.ku: نەخۆشییەکی باکتریایی درێژخایەن کە سکاندنی درەنگ، نەزۆکی و ئاوسانی جومگە دروست دەکات. نەخۆشییەکی گرنگی گوازرەوە بۆ مرۆڤ و کێشەیەکی گەورەی ئاژەڵداری و بازرگانییە.
summary.ar: عدوى بكتيرية مزمنة تسبب الإجهاض المتأخر والعقم وتورم المفاصل. وهي مرض حيواني المنشأ مهم للصحة العامة والتجارة.

diseases.zoonoticNote: Yes. People can be infected through contact with birth fluids, placenta, urine or raw milk. Wear gloves and eye protection when handling calving; seek urgent medical advice after exposure. Pregnant women need special caution.
diseases.notifiableNote: Usually notifiable and subject to official test-and-slaughter or vaccination programmes. Report abortions and positive tests according to national rules.
diseases.meatNote: Brucellosis is zoonotic; carcasses of infected animals are subject to official condemnation and handling regulations.
diseases.causativeAgent: Brucella abortus is the main cattle pathogen. B. melitensis and B. suis can also infect cattle and people. Bacteria are shed in birth fluids, placenta, milk and urine.
diseases.affected: Cattle, especially sexually mature heifers and cows in mid-to-late gestation. Bulls can develop orchitis. Some infected animals show no signs and remain carriers.
symptoms: Late-term abortion and stillbirth
Retained placenta and uterine infection
Weak calves and reduced fertility
Swollen scrotum and orchitis in bulls
Swollen joints and enlarged lymph nodes
Few or no other signs; carrier animals can calve normally
diseases.diagnosis: Use validated serological tests such as the Rose Bengal test, ELISA or complement fixation, followed by culture or PCR on abortion material, milk or tissues. All sampling must follow official protocols. Distinguish vaccination reactions from infection.
diseases.postMortem: Abortion is often accompanied by retained, thickened and inflamed foetal membranes that may look leathery and yellow-brown. The foetus may show subcutaneous oedema, serosanguineous cavity fluid, enlarged liver and spleen, and bronchopneumonia. Bulls can have epididymitis, orchitis and swollen scrotal tissue. Handle all reproductive material with gloves and official biosecurity because brucellosis is zoonotic.
diseases.treatment: There is no practical treatment for cattle. Control relies on test-and-slaughter, vaccination and movement restrictions as directed by the official programme. People with suspected brucellosis need medical diagnosis and a full course of combination antibiotics.
diseases.prevention: Test and remove infected animals, quarantine introduced cattle, control movements and handle calving hygienically. Pasteurise milk and dairy products. Eligible heifers may be vaccinated with approved vaccines under a national programme; vaccination alone does not replace surveillance.

summary.en: A chronic bacterial disease of cattle that mainly affects the lungs and lymph nodes. It can spread to wildlife and people and is controlled through official testing programmes.
summary.ku: نەخۆشییەکی باکتریایی درێژخایەنە کە بە شێوەیەکی سەرەکی سی و گرێی لیمفاوی تووش دەکات. دەتوانێت بۆ ئاژەڵی کێوی و مرۆڤ بگوازرێتەوە.
summary.ar: مرض بكتيري مزمن يصيب الرئتين والعقد اللمفاوية بشكل رئيسي. يمكن أن ينتقل إلى الحياة البرية والإنسان ويخضع لبرامج فحص رسمية.

diseases.zoonoticNote: Yes. People can be infected by inhaling infectious droplets or drinking unpasteurised milk, especially from infected cattle. Pasteurisation greatly reduces foodborne risk.
diseases.notifiableNote: Notifiable in most countries, with compulsory testing, movement controls and slaughter of reactors under official supervision.
diseases.meatNote: Bovine tuberculosis is a severe zoonosis; carcasses showing lesions are condemned under official meat inspection rules.
diseases.causativeAgent: Mycobacterium bovis, a slow-growing bacterium related to the human tuberculosis organism. Infection may remain latent for months or years.
diseases.affected: Cattle of all ages, particularly adults in affected herds. Deer, badgers and other wildlife can act as reservoirs in some regions. Humans and other mammals are also susceptible.
symptoms: Progressive weight loss and poor body condition
A chronic cough, often worse after exercise
Enlarged lymph nodes, especially around the head and neck
Intermittent low-grade fever and reduced appetite
Reduced milk yield and fertility
Often no obvious signs in early or latent infection
diseases.diagnosis: Official testing typically uses the single intradermal tuberculin skin test and may include the interferon-gamma test. Post-mortem examination, culture and PCR confirm infection. Do not attempt home diagnosis.
diseases.postMortem: Yellow-white caseous granulomas, often with calcification, in the lungs and bronchial or mediastinal lymph nodes; lesions may also involve the liver, spleen, kidneys, pleura, peritoneum, udder and intestine. Lesions can be small and easily missed. Submit fresh and fixed tissue for culture and PCR under official biosecurity because M. bovis can infect people.
diseases.treatment: Cattle are normally not treated; eradication programmes use test-and-slaughter. Infected animals must be handled under official rules. People with suspected tuberculosis need specialist medical assessment and multi-drug treatment.
diseases.prevention: Participate in routine testing and surveillance, restrict contact with wildlife reservoirs, maintain herd biosecurity and pasteurise milk. BCG vaccination of cattle is not routinely used and only applies in specific research or official programmes.

summary.en: A viral infection with many faces: diarrhoea, respiratory signs, reproductive loss and persistent infection in calves. Identifying persistently infected animals is central to control.
summary.ku: نەخۆشییەکی ڤایرۆسییە و دەرکەوتنی جیاوازی هەیە: سکچوون، نیشانەی هەناسەدان، لەدەستدانی زاوزێ و تووشبوونی هەمیشەیی لە گوێرەکان. دۆزینەوەی ئاژەڵی تووشبووی هەمیشەیی بنەمای کۆنترۆڵە.
summary.ar: عدوى فيروسية متعددة المظاهر تشمل الإسهال ومشاكل التنفس وخسائر التكاثر والإصابة المستمرة في العجول. تحديد الحيوانات المصابة بشكل دائم أساسي للمكافحة.

diseases.zoonoticNote: Not a human pathogen. Normal hygiene is still recommended when handling sick animals and birth fluids.
diseases.notifiableNote: Not OIE-listed as a whole, but reporting requirements vary by country and some regional control programmes are mandatory.
diseases.meatNote: Meat from recovered or non-febrile animals is fit for consumption after routine post-mortem inspection and drug withdrawal.
diseases.causativeAgent: Bovine viral diarrhoea virus, a pestivirus. Transient infection is temporary, but infection of a foetus in early pregnancy can create a persistently infected calf that sheds virus for life.
diseases.affected: Cattle of all ages. Persistently infected (PI) calves are the main reservoir. Susceptible breeding cattle and young stock in mixed groups are at particular risk.
symptoms: Fever, lethargy and reduced appetite
Diarrhoea, sometimes blood-stained
Erosions or ulcers in the mouth, nose and on the feet
Cough, nasal discharge and rapid breathing when respiratory disease is involved
Abortion, stillbirth, weak calves and poor fertility
Poor growth or chronic ill thrift in PI animals; some PI cattle look normal
diseases.diagnosis: Detect virus with PCR or antigen ELISA in blood, milk or tissue, and use serology to assess herd exposure. PI animals require repeat testing after an appropriate interval. Work with a veterinarian to design a representative herd sample.
diseases.postMortem: Lesions vary with age and strain. Erosions and ulcers may occur in the mouth, oesophagus, rumen, abomasum and intestine, with congestion, haemorrhage and depletion of lymphoid tissue. Persistently infected animals may be stunted or have no gross lesions. Aborted foetuses may show cerebellar hypoplasia, oedema or no changes; submit spleen, lymph node, intestine and foetal tissue for PCR.
diseases.treatment: No specific antiviral is available. Give supportive nursing and fluids, and use antibiotics only for confirmed or strongly suspected secondary bacterial pneumonia. Isolate and test PI suspects to prevent ongoing transmission.
diseases.prevention: Use biosecurity, quarantine and testing of introduced cattle, identify and remove PI animals, and protect young stock with good colostrum. Vaccination may be part of an approved national or herd control programme; vaccine use alone will not clear PI cattle.

summary.en: A capripoxvirus infection of cattle causing fever and firm skin nodules, with significant milk and fertility losses. It spreads mainly through biting insects.
summary.ku: نەخۆشییەکی ڤایرۆسی (کاپریپۆکس)ی مانگایە کە تا و گرێی ڕەقی پێست دروست دەکات و شیر و زاوزێ کەم دەکات. بە شێوەیەکی سەرەکی بە مێش و مێرووی گازلێدەر بڵاو دەبێتەوە.
summary.ar: عدوى فيروسية من مجموعة كابريبوكس تصيب الأبقار وتسبب الحمى وعقداً جلدية صلبة، مع خسائر في الحليب والخصوبة. ينتشر بشكل رئيسي عبر الحشرات القارصة.

diseases.zoonoticNote: Not known to infect people. Wear gloves when handling open skin lesions because secondary bacteria can cause infection.
diseases.notifiableNote: WOAH-listed and reportable in affected and at-risk countries. Immediate reporting is essential because vaccination and movement controls can limit spread.
diseases.meatNote: Lumpy skin disease is reportable; affected animals with fever, generalized nodules, or secondary infection are condemned at slaughter.
diseases.causativeAgent: Lumpy skin disease virus, a capripoxvirus. Biting flies, mosquitoes and ticks transmit it mechanically; contaminated needles, equipment and semen can also spread infection.
diseases.affected: Cattle and water buffalo of all ages. High-producing dairy cattle and young calves often develop more severe disease. Sheep and goats are not affected by LSD virus.
symptoms: Fever and enlarged lymph nodes
Firm, round skin nodules, typically 1–5 cm, on the head, neck, back, udder and legs
Nodules that ulcerate, form scabs or become secondarily infected
Swelling of the legs and lameness
Milk drop, infertility and poor body condition
Nasal or eye discharge and lesions inside the mouth
diseases.diagnosis: PCR on skin nodules, scabs, blood or semen is the usual confirmation, with virus isolation in reference laboratories. Collect samples only with official guidance. Report suspected cases before moving animals.
diseases.postMortem: Firm, raised skin nodules up to several centimetres across involve the dermis and sometimes underlying muscle; they may ulcerate or become necrotic. Oedema of the limbs and brisket, enlarged lymph nodes and lesions in the mouth, pharynx, trachea and udder can occur. Internal nodules may affect the respiratory and digestive tracts. Submit skin and lymph node samples for PCR and rule out other pox diseases.
diseases.treatment: No specific antiviral treatment exists. Provide nursing care, soft feed, wound and fly management, NSAIDs and antibiotics for secondary bacterial infection only under veterinary direction.
diseases.prevention: Vaccinate with an approved LSD vaccine where available and permitted. Control biting insects, quarantine new animals, avoid shared needles and follow official movement restrictions. Vaccination is most useful before transmission begins.

summary.en: A serious soil-borne bacterial disease that can cause sudden death and bloody discharge. It is a zoonosis, and suspicious carcasses must never be opened without official advice.
summary.ku: نەخۆشییەکی باکتریایی گرنگە کە لە خاکەوە دێت و دەتوانێت مردنی لەناکاو و دەردانی خوێناوی دروست بکات. نەخۆشییەکی مرۆڤیشە؛ تەرمی گومانلێکراو نابێت بەبێ ڕێنمایی فەرمی بکرێتەوە.
summary.ar: مرض بكتيري خطير يوجد في التربة وقد يسبب موتاً مفاجئاً وإفرازات دموية. وهو مرض حيواني المنشأ، ولا يجوز تشريح جثث مشتبهة دون إرشاد رسمي.

diseases.zoonoticNote: Yes, a serious zoonosis. Spores can enter through broken skin, inhalation or ingestion. Do not open carcasses, burn or bury without official guidance, and see a doctor urgently after contact.
diseases.notifiableNote: Emergency reportable in almost all countries. Contact veterinary and public-health authorities immediately; a dead animal with unexplained bleeding must be treated as suspected anthrax.
diseases.meatNote: Do not slaughter or butcher animals suspected of anthrax. Carcasses must never be opened or consumed; anthrax is a fatal zoonosis.
diseases.causativeAgent: Bacillus anthracis, a spore-forming bacterium. Spores survive for decades in contaminated soil and can be stirred up by flooding, digging or grazing.
diseases.affected: Cattle and sheep of all ages, especially grazing animals in endemic areas. People and many other mammals are susceptible.
symptoms: Sudden death, often the first and only sign
High fever and rapid collapse in the short course
Bloodstained discharge from the nose, mouth, anus or vulva; blood may not clot
Breathing difficulty and colicky signs
Soft swelling of the neck, throat, brisket or perineum
Failure to respond quickly to treatment
diseases.diagnosis: Do not perform a standard necropsy. Report immediately and let authorised staff collect blood or ear-notch samples for staining, culture or PCR at an official laboratory. A blood smear showing encapsulated rods supports the diagnosis.
diseases.postMortem: Suspected anthrax must never be opened. The classic finding is dark, tarry, incompletely clotted blood from body openings, with rapid bloating and decomposition. Blood smears show square-ended, encapsulated bacilli. If a carcass is opened, massive splenomegaly, haemorrhages and oedematous enteritis may be seen, but this creates a serious human and environmental hazard. Notify the authorities before any handling and do not perform a field necropsy.
diseases.treatment: Early high-dose antibiotics can save animals in the very early stage, but treatment must be directed by the official veterinary service. Carcasses should be incinerated or buried deep with lime according to regulations. Exposed people require urgent medical evaluation and prophylaxis.
diseases.prevention: Vaccinate livestock in endemic areas on a regular schedule and manage outbreaks under official control. Avoid grazing known contaminated sites, do not move carcasses, and use full PPE during any official sampling or disposal. Spores persist in soil for decades.

summary.en: A rapidly fatal clostridial infection of muscle in young, well-conditioned cattle. Early signs are often missed and sudden death is common.
summary.ku: نەخۆشییەکی کلۆستریدیالی زۆر خێرا کوشندەیە کە ماسولکەی گوێرە گەنج و قەڵەو تووش دەکات. زۆرجار نیشانەکان لە دەست دەچن و مردنی لەناکاو باوە.
summary.ar: عدوى كلوستريدية سريعة وقاتلة تصيب عضلات العجول الصغيرة ذات الحالة الجيدة. غالباً ما تفوت العلامات المبكرة ويحدث موت مفاجئ.

diseases.zoonoticNote: Not a zoonosis. Use gloves when handling carcasses or affected tissue to protect against other bacteria.
diseases.notifiableNote: Not usually reportable, but anthrax must be excluded before any carcass is opened because the two diseases can look similar.
diseases.meatNote: Carcasses of animals affected by or dying from blackleg are toxic, contaminated, and strictly condemned; never consume the meat.
diseases.causativeAgent: Clostridium chauvoei, a spore-forming bacterium. Spores can lie dormant in muscle and gut-associated tissues and activate after bruising or a change in gut conditions.
diseases.affected: Young cattle, usually 6 months to 2 years old, in good condition. Outbreaks can follow vaccination injections, trauma or sudden pasture/feed changes. Sheep are affected less commonly.
symptoms: Sudden severe lameness with a hot, painful muscle swelling, often in a hind leg or shoulder
Crackling under the skin as gas forms
Dark, cold skin over the swollen area
Fever, depression and rapid breathing
Rapid collapse and death, often within 12–48 hours
diseases.diagnosis: The history and post-mortem findings are characteristic: blackened, gas-filled muscle with a rancid smell. Confirm with culture or PCR on affected tissue. Rule out anthrax before opening any carcass, and seek veterinary help with safe sampling.
diseases.postMortem: The carcass decomposes quickly and is often bloated, with dark, swollen muscle groups in the hindquarters, shoulder or back. Affected muscle is dark red to black, friable and spongy, with a rancid smell and gas bubbles; subcutaneous oedema and haemorrhage are common. Blood-stained fluid may escape from natural openings. Rule out anthrax before opening the carcass; collect affected muscle and exudate for culture or PCR.
diseases.treatment: Treatment is often too late because the disease progresses rapidly. Very early high-dose antibiotics and supportive care may be attempted under immediate veterinary direction. Do not delay to try home treatments.
diseases.prevention: Vaccinate calves with a clostridial vaccine containing C. chauvoei and give boosters according to the label. Avoid sudden high-grain feeding, reduce bruising and manage pastures. Handle carcasses safely and investigate the source of infection.

summary.en: Rapid accumulation of gas in the rumen causes a distended abdomen, breathing difficulty and possible death. Frothy bloat from lush legumes is a common emergency.
summary.ku: کۆبوونەوەی خێرای گاز لە ڕومین دەبێتە هۆی ئاوسانی سک، سەختێی هەناسەدان و لەوانەیە مردن. ئاوسانی کەفکی لە لەگی شێوەدار زۆرجار حاڵەتێکی فریاکەوتنە.
summary.ar: تراكم سريع للغازات في الكرش يسبب انتفاخ البطن وصعوبة التنفس وقد يؤدي إلى الموت. الانتفاخ الرغوي الناتج عن الأعلاف البقولية الغضة حالة طارئة شائعة.

diseases.zoonoticNote: Not a zoonosis.
diseases.notifiableNote: Not notifiable.
diseases.meatNote: Animals dying of bloat are unfit for consumption. Emergency slaughter is only permitted under strict ante-mortem veterinary supervision.
diseases.causativeAgent: Excessive gas production and impaired eructation. Frothy bloat usually follows sudden access to lush legumes such as clover or alfalfa. Free-gas bloat can result from oesophageal obstruction, vagal nerve damage or other rumen outflow problems.
diseases.affected: Cattle and sheep, especially hungry animals suddenly turned onto lush legume pasture or feedlot cattle on high-concentrate diets. Adults are most commonly affected; calves can bloat after milk or feed problems.
symptoms: Rapidly distended left flank with a tight, drum-like abdomen
Discomfort, kicking at the belly and reduced rumination
Rapid, shallow or open-mouth breathing
Drooling, grunting or straining
Reluctance to move, staggering and eventual collapse
Death from respiratory and circulatory compromise in severe cases
diseases.diagnosis: Diagnose from the distended flank, drum-like sound, feeding history and breathing effort. A stomach tube may distinguish free gas from froth and can reveal an obstruction. Severe bloat requires immediate veterinary assessment; do not delay for laboratory tests.
diseases.postMortem: Marked ruminal distension with a tense left flank; the carcass may be found in lateral recumbency. The rumen is hugely distended with foam or free gas and pushes the diaphragm forward. Lung congestion and abomasal displacement may be present. Examine the rumen contents and rule out choke, obstruction and anthrax before attributing death to bloat.
diseases.treatment: This is an emergency. A stomach tube can relieve free gas but may not clear froth. Antifoaming agents may be used under veterinary advice. Emergency rumen puncture or trocarisation should only be performed by trained personnel. Treat any underlying choke or feed problem.
diseases.prevention: Introduce livestock gradually to lush legume pasture, provide adequate long roughage, avoid turning hungry animals onto wet clover and manage feedlot rations carefully. Monitor high-risk animals daily and use approved bloat-prevention strategies.

summary.en: A metabolic disorder around calving caused by low blood calcium. Early signs are subtle; untreated cows can go down and die.
summary.ku: نەخۆشییەکی میتابۆلیکی دەوری سکاندنە کە بەهۆی کەمی کالسیۆم لە خوێن دروست دەبێت. نیشانە سەرەتاییەکان وردن؛ ئەگەر چارەسەر نەکرێت مانگا دەکەوێت و دەمرێت.
summary.ar: اضطراب أيضي حول الولادة بسبب انخفاض الكالسيوم في الدم. العلامات المبكرة خفية، وإذا لم تعالج فقد تسقط البقرة وتموت.

diseases.zoonoticNote: Not a zoonosis.
diseases.notifiableNote: Not notifiable.
diseases.meatNote: Cows that recover completely from milk fever and pass ante- and post-mortem inspection produce safe meat, provided no restricted drugs were given.
diseases.causativeAgent: A sudden fall in blood calcium due to the onset of lactation. Risk increases with high potassium or high calcium transition diets, older age, high milk yield and overconditioning.
diseases.affected: Dairy cows, most often within 24 hours before to 72 hours after calving. Older, high-producing cows are at greater risk. Ewes and goats can also develop hypocalcaemia.
symptoms: Staggering, muscle trembling and weakness
Cold extremities and a curved neck, sometimes called an S-shape
A downer cow that cannot rise
Dullness, reduced gut sounds and scanty droppings
Rapid shallow breathing and collapse in advanced cases
Death if untreated; a cow may also be down for other reasons
diseases.diagnosis: Suspect from the timing and signs, and confirm with blood calcium and magnesium/phosphorus measurements. A positive response to calcium treatment supports the diagnosis but does not replace a full examination. Rule out mastitis, metritis and other downer-cow causes.
diseases.postMortem: There are often no specific gross lesions; the animal may be found in sternal recumbency with a cold, unresponsive appearance. Congestion of the abomasum and lungs and a distended bladder may be seen. Low serum calcium supports the diagnosis if a sample was taken before treatment. Necropsy mainly helps exclude mastitis, metritis, ketosis, trauma and other causes of recumbency.
diseases.treatment: Urgent intravenous calcium under veterinary supervision is the standard treatment; give it slowly and monitor the heart. Oral calcium and careful nursing may follow. Do not attempt IV injections without training, and consider magnesium deficiency if the cow does not respond.
diseases.prevention: Use a balanced transition ration with controlled dietary cation-anion difference, avoid overconditioning and ensure adequate magnesium. Manage calcium intake carefully and use targeted preventive strategies under veterinary advice. Examine downer cows promptly.

summary.en: A metabolic disease of early lactation caused by negative energy balance. Cows lose appetite, milk and condition, and develop ketones in blood and urine.
summary.ku: نەخۆشییەکی میتابۆلیکی سەرەتای شیردانییە کە بەهۆی کەمی وزەی وەرگیراو دروست دەبێت. مانگا ئیشتە، شیر و کێش لەدەست دەدات و کیتۆن لە خوێن و میزدا دروست دەبێت.
summary.ar: مرض أيضي في بداية الإدرار بسبب توازن طاقة سلبي. تفقد البقرة الشهية والحليب والحالة الجسمية وتتراكم الكيتونات في الدم والبول.

diseases.zoonoticNote: Not a zoonosis.
diseases.notifiableNote: Not notifiable.
diseases.meatNote: Recovered animals passing routine meat inspection are fit for slaughter. Severely emaciated animals or those with heavy ketone odor are condemned.
diseases.causativeAgent: Severe negative energy balance after calving leads to mobilisation of body fat and overproduction of ketones. Overconditioning, twin pregnancy, poor transition feeding and concurrent diseases increase risk.
diseases.affected: Dairy cows in early lactation, especially the first 6–8 weeks after calving. Overfat cows and cows with metritis, retained placenta or a displaced abomasum are at higher risk.
symptoms: Decreased appetite and a sudden fall in milk yield
Sweet, acetone-like smell on the breath or milk
Weight loss despite access to feed
Dullness, reduced rumination and firm, dry droppings
Nervous signs, tremors or recumbency in severe cases
Poor fertility later in lactation
diseases.diagnosis: Test urine or milk with a ketone strip, or measure blood beta-hydroxybutyrate (BHB). Examine the cow fully for a concurrent disease such as metritis, mastitis or displaced abomasum. Herd monitoring of BHB in early-lactation cows is valuable.
diseases.postMortem: The carcass is often emaciated with depleted fat reserves and a pale, enlarged, greasy liver. The rumen may be underfilled and an abomasal displacement can coexist. Early cases may have no specific gross lesions. Look for metritis, mastitis, displaced abomasum and pregnancy toxaemia, and submit liver and blood for supportive testing.
diseases.treatment: Provide a rapidly available energy source such as intravenous glucose or oral propylene glycol under veterinary direction. Correct dehydration and concurrent disease, and encourage palatable feed. Monitor response and repeat BHB testing if signs persist.
diseases.prevention: Prevent overfat cows at calving and support a smooth transition with adequate dry-matter intake and balanced energy/protein. Monitor body condition and early-lactation BHB. Treat other calving-related problems promptly and review the total mixed ration with a nutritionist.

summary.en: A tick-borne protozoal disease that attacks white blood cells and red cells, causing fever, swollen lymph nodes, anaemia and sometimes sudden death.
summary.ku: نەخۆشییەکی پڕۆتۆزۆییە کە بە مێش دەگوازرێتەوە و خانەکانی خوێن سپی و خانە سوورەکان تووش دەکات؛ تا، ئاوسانی گرێی لیمفاوی، کەمی خوێن و هەندێکجار مردنی لەناکاو دروست دەکات.
summary.ar: مرض طفيلي ينتقل بالقراد ويصيب كريات الدم البيضاء والحمراء، مسبباً الحمى وتضخم العقد اللمفاوية وفقر الدم وأحياناً الموت المفاجئ.

diseases.zoonoticNote: Not a zoonosis. Tick-control measures still protect people from other tick-borne diseases.
diseases.notifiableNote: Reportability varies by country and Theileria species. East Coast fever is subject to official control where it occurs.
diseases.meatNote: Animals with acute theileriosis showing fever, jaundice, or severe anaemia are condemned at slaughter inspection.
diseases.causativeAgent: Theileria parva causes East Coast fever; T. annulata causes tropical theileriosis. Both are protozoa transmitted by ticks. Infected cattle can remain carriers.
diseases.affected: Cattle, with severe disease common in exotic and naive animals moved into endemic areas. Calves and young stock may be especially susceptible depending on species and prior exposure.
symptoms: High fever and enlarged lymph nodes
Depression, poor appetite and weight loss
Rapid or difficult breathing and nasal discharge
Pale mucous membranes, sometimes jaundice
Diarrhoea, nervous signs or sudden death in severe cases
Abortion and a sharp drop in milk production
diseases.diagnosis: Examine blood smears and lymph-node aspirates for parasites and use PCR for confirmation and species identification. Distinguish from babesiosis and anaplasmosis, which can occur together. Contact the veterinary service if East Coast fever is suspected.
diseases.postMortem: Pale mucous membranes and jaundice, with enlarged lymph nodes, spleen and liver. The abomasum and intestines may show erosions and haemorrhage, and the lungs can be oedematous. In East Coast fever, pulmonary oedema, interstitial emphysema and marked lymphoid enlargement are common. Examine stained smears from lymph node, spleen or blood for piroplasms and collect tissue for PCR.
diseases.treatment: Specific anti-theilerial drugs such as buparvaquone are available only through veterinary direction and must be given early. Provide supportive fluids and nursing care. Carrier animals need specialist advice because treatment does not always clear infection.
diseases.prevention: Control ticks with an appropriate strategic programme, use available vaccination (for example East Coast fever immunisation) where licensed, and quarantine or test introduced cattle. Avoid sharing needles and blood-contaminated equipment. Breeding for tolerance can help in endemic regions.

summary.en: A tick-borne parasite that destroys red blood cells, causing fever, anaemia, jaundice and dark red urine. It can be fatal in adult cattle.
summary.ku: پەرازیتێکە کە بە مێش دەگوازرێتەوە و خانە سوورەکانی خوێن لەناو دەبات؛ تا، کەمی خوێن، زەردبوون و میزی سووری تاریک دروست دەکات. دەتوانێت بۆ مانگای گەورە کوشندە بێت.
summary.ar: طفيل ينتقل بالقراد ويدمر كريات الدم الحمراء، مسبباً الحمى وفقر الدم واليرقان والبول الأحمر الداكن. قد يكون قاتلاً لدى الأبقار البالغة.

diseases.zoonoticNote: Cattle Babesia species are not a human zoonosis, but tick bites can transmit other diseases to people.
diseases.notifiableNote: Not usually notifiable, though national rules vary.
diseases.meatNote: Carcasses with jaundice, anaemia, or redwater haemoglobinuria from acute babesiosis are unfit and condemned.
diseases.causativeAgent: Babesia bovis, B. bigemina and B. divergens are protozoal parasites of red blood cells transmitted by ticks, mainly Rhipicephalus species.
diseases.affected: Cattle of all ages. Adults moved into endemic areas are often severely affected; calves may have some protection from colostrum. Infection can persist in carrier animals.
symptoms: High fever, lethargy and reduced appetite
Dark red or brown urine
Pale or yellow mucous membranes due to anaemia and jaundice
Weakness, rapid breathing and a rapid heartbeat
Abortion or collapse in severe cases
Reduced milk yield and ill thrift
diseases.diagnosis: Examine a blood smear for parasites inside red cells, and use PCR or serology when available. Monitor red-cell count and kidney function. The disease must be distinguished from other tick-borne diseases and from leptospirosis.
diseases.postMortem: The carcass is anaemic and jaundiced, with pale mucous membranes and thin, watery blood. The spleen and liver are enlarged and the gall bladder may be distended. Petechial haemorrhages and haemoglobin-stained urine in the bladder can occur. Examine blood, spleen or kidney impression smears for Babesia and rule out anaplasmosis and theileriosis.
diseases.treatment: Specific anti-babesial drugs such as imidocarb are given under veterinary supervision, with supportive fluids and sometimes a blood transfusion. Early treatment improves survival. Do not use unlicensed products or guess doses.
diseases.prevention: Use strategic tick control, inspect animals regularly and avoid moving naive cattle into high-risk areas without advice. Vaccination may be available in some countries. Test introduced animals and keep needles and blood-contaminated items separate.

summary.en: A liver fluke infection acquired from wet pasture and snail habitats. It causes ill thrift, anaemia and reduced milk production, and is also a human food-safety concern.
summary.ku: نەخۆشییەکی کرمی جگەرە کە لە لەوەڕی شێدار و شوێنی لوولۆکەکان وەردەگیرێت. بەهۆی کەمی گەشە، کەمی خوێن و کەمبوونی شیر دەناسرێت و بۆ سەلامەتی خواردنی مرۆڤیش گرنگە.
summary.ar: عدوى دودة الكبد المكتسبة من المراعي الرطبة وموائل القواقع. تسبب ضعف النمو وفقر الدم وانخفاض الحليب، وهي أيضاً مشكلة سلامة غذائية للإنسان.

diseases.zoonoticNote: Yes, humans can get fascioliosis by eating contaminated aquatic plants or drinking contaminated water. Cattle are not directly infectious to people; control snails and avoid contaminated watercress or water sources.
diseases.notifiableNote: Not usually notifiable in livestock, though human cases may be reportable locally.
diseases.meatNote: Meat from healthy muscle is safe after official inspection. Condemnation is limited to the affected liver unless severe emaciation is present.
diseases.causativeAgent: Fasciola hepatica and F. gigantica are flatworms that migrate through liver tissue and live in bile ducts. Freshwater snails are essential intermediate hosts and release infective stages onto wet grass.
diseases.affected: Cattle, sheep and goats, especially grazing young stock and animals on wet pasture. Adult cattle often carry chronic infections. Sheep can die from heavy acute infections.
symptoms: Weight loss and poor growth
Pale membranes and anaemia
Bottle-jaw swelling under the jaw caused by low protein
Diarrhoea and reduced appetite
Reduced milk yield and poor fertility
Jaundice and severe disease in heavy infections
diseases.diagnosis: Use faecal egg sedimentation or a coproantigen ELISA; serology can help detect early or acute exposure in sheep. Abattoir liver inspection is useful. Sample a representative group rather than only visibly thin animals.
diseases.postMortem: In acute disease the liver is swollen with subcapsular haemorrhages and necrotic tracks; chronic disease causes fibrosis, thickened bile ducts and sometimes a distended gall bladder. Flukes may be visible in the bile ducts or liver parenchyma. Emaciation and jaundice may be present. Examine the liver and bile ducts directly and use faecal sedimentation to confirm exposure.
diseases.treatment: Use an appropriate flukicide under veterinary direction. Triclabendazole is effective against immature fluke in some species, but resistance and local restrictions exist. Support nutrition and treat anaemia; observe milk and meat withdrawal periods.
diseases.prevention: Fence or drain wet snail habitats, avoid grazing high-risk wet pasture at peak times and use strategic seasonal treatments based on local risk. Provide clean water and feed. Protect people by avoiding raw aquatic plants from contaminated areas.

summary.en: A multifactorial respiratory disease complex, especially after transport and mixing. Stress, viruses and bacteria combine to cause pneumonia, poor growth and losses.
summary.ku: نەخۆشییەکی ئاڵۆزی هەناسەدانە، بەتایبەتی دوای گواستنەوە و تێکەڵکردنی ئاژەڵ. سترێس، ڤایرۆس و باکتریا پێکەوە سیەسۆیل و کەمگەشە دروست دەکەن.
summary.ar: مرض تنفسي مركب متعدد العوامل، خاصة بعد النقل والخلط. تجتمع الضغوط والفيروسات والبكتيريا لتسبب الالتهاب الرئوي وضعف النمو والخسائر.

diseases.zoonoticNote: The usual cattle respiratory pathogens are not a public-health zoonosis. Some pathogens can infect people with close contact, so maintain hygiene.
diseases.notifiableNote: Not usually notifiable as a syndrome, but specific pathogens such as tuberculosis or vesicular diseases must be excluded.
diseases.meatNote: Meat from fully recovered cattle is fit after routine meat inspection and observance of drug withdrawal times.
diseases.causativeAgent: Mannheimia haemolytica, Pasteurella multocida, Histophilus somni and Mycoplasma bovis act alongside viruses such as BRSV, parainfluenza-3, IBR and BVDV. Poor ventilation, crowding, transport, weaning and dust are major triggers.
diseases.affected: Cattle of all ages, most often recently weaned, transported or mixed calves and feedlot cattle. Indoor and poorly ventilated groups are at high risk.
symptoms: Cough, especially after movement
Fast or shallow breathing and flared nostrils
Fever, depression and reduced appetite
Nasal and eye discharge
Weight loss and poor growth
Ear droop or head tilt if the middle ear is involved
diseases.diagnosis: Assess temperature, breathing effort and lung sounds, and use a standard clinical scoring system. In outbreaks, collect appropriate nasal or lung samples for pathogen testing. Review ventilation, stocking density and mixing practices.
diseases.postMortem: Consolidated, dark-red to grey lung lobules, usually cranioventral, with frothy or purulent airway exudate; pleurisy and abscesses may be present. Bronchial and mediastinal lymph nodes are enlarged. Severe cases may show fibrin, necrosis and extensive adhesions. Collect lung, airway swabs and lymph nodes for bacterial and viral testing; gross lesions alone do not identify the cause.
diseases.treatment: Promptly examine affected animals and provide anti-inflammatory support, fluids and good nursing. Use antibiotics only when bacterial pneumonia is likely, following local guidelines and culture where possible. Isolate sick calves and avoid untargeted group treatment.
diseases.prevention: Ensure good colostrum and calf health, provide ventilation and low-dust bedding, avoid overcrowding, reduce transport stress and use quarantine for new stock. Vaccination should be tailored to the pathogens and risk periods in the herd.

summary.en: Infectious diarrhoea in young calves that quickly causes dehydration and acidosis. Poor colostrum, dirty bedding and mixed pathogens are common drivers.
summary.ku: سکچوونی تووشکەر لە گوێرە گەنجەکاندا کە بە خێرایی وشکبوون و ترشی خوێن دروست دەکات. کەمی کۆلۆسترۆم، جێگای پیس و تێکەڵبوونی چەند هۆکار هۆکاری باون.
summary.ar: إسهال معدٍ في العجول الصغيرة يسبب الجفاف والحُماض بسرعة. ضعف اللبأ والفراش الملوث واختلاط العوامل الممرضة أسباب شائعة.

diseases.zoonoticNote: Some causes such as Cryptosporidium and Salmonella can affect people. Wear gloves, wash hands and do not allow children to handle scouring calves.
diseases.notifiableNote: Not usually notifiable, but Salmonella and other pathogens may require local reporting.
diseases.meatNote: Recovered calves passing inspection are fit for consumption after drug withdrawal periods. Severely dehydrated or septic calves are condemned.
diseases.causativeAgent: Rotavirus, coronavirus, E. coli, Cryptosporidium, Salmonella and Clostridium perfringens are common, often in combination. Failure of passive transfer, overcrowding and poor hygiene make disease more severe.
diseases.affected: Neonatal calves, typically 1–21 days old. Calves with inadequate colostrum, difficult births, cold stress or dirty calving environments are most at risk.
symptoms: Watery diarrhoea, sometimes blood-stained
Sunken eyes, dry mouth and a slow skin tent from dehydration
Weakness, reluctance to suck and a cold mouth or legs
Reduced urine output and progressing collapse
Abdominal discomfort
Death from dehydration or acidosis if treatment is delayed
diseases.diagnosis: Assess hydration, suck reflex, temperature and acidosis. Faecal tests can identify Cryptosporidium, Salmonella or viruses, and herd investigation should review colostrum management and hygiene. Blood gas analysis is useful in severe cases.
diseases.postMortem: Dehydration, sunken eyes and dry tissues are usually more obvious than gut lesions. The abomasum and intestines may be congested and thin-walled, with watery or blood-stained contents; rotavirus and coronavirus often cause only mild small-intestinal changes, while E. coli and Salmonella can produce fibrinous or haemorrhagic enteritis. Check for coccidiosis and cryptosporidiosis, and submit gut and content for culture and PCR.
diseases.treatment: Start oral electrolyte fluids immediately and continue milk or milk replacer. Severe dehydration or a depressed calf needs intravenous fluids. Do not use antibiotics routinely; use them only for specific bacterial causes under veterinary guidance. Isolate sick calves.
diseases.prevention: Ensure adequate high-quality colostrum within the first hours of life, then consistent clean feeding. Clean and disinfect calving pens, use dry bedding, isolate sick calves and avoid overcrowding. Vaccinating dams according to label can reduce some causes.

summary.en: Lameness is a sign, not one disease. Hoof lesions, joint disease, injuries and laminitis all cause pain, reduced feeding and lower milk yield.
summary.ku: لەنگبوون نیشانەیەکە، نەک یەک نەخۆشی. برینی سم، نەخۆشی جومگە، برین و لامینایتیس هەموویان ئازار، کەمی خواردن و کەمبوونی شیر دروست دەکەن.
summary.ar: العرج علامة وليس مرضاً واحداً. آفات الحافر وأمراض المفاصل والإصابات والتهاب الصفيحة تسبب الألم وقلة الأكل وانخفاض الحليب.

diseases.zoonoticNote: Not a zoonosis. Treat infected foot wounds with gloves because bacteria in manure can infect human skin.
diseases.notifiableNote: Not usually notifiable; report specific infectious foot diseases if local rules require.
diseases.meatNote: Carcass muscle is safe after feet trimming and routine inspection, provided there is no systemic infection or active drug residue.
diseases.causativeAgent: Common causes include digital dermatitis, sole ulcers, white line disease, foot rot, laminitis, joint infection and injury. Wet, dirty housing, long standing times, poor hoof trimming and rumen acidosis are important risk factors.
diseases.affected: Cattle of all ages, especially adult dairy and feedlot cattle. Heavy cows, wet climates and cubicle housing with poor comfort are at higher risk.
symptoms: Reluctance to walk, short strides and a head bob
Arched back and uneven weight-bearing
A swollen, warm or painful foot or joint
Sores, separation of the hoof wall or discharge
Reduced feed intake, body condition and milk yield
Culling risk when chronic
diseases.diagnosis: Examine the standing and walking cow, then lift each foot in a safe crush and inspect the sole, heel and interdigital space. Use a herd mobility score and investigate housing and ration. Radiographs or ultrasound may help with deep infection.
diseases.postMortem: Findings depend on the cause. Interdigital skin is eroded, swollen and foul-smelling in foot rot, while sole abscess or white line disease leaves a necrotic tract under the sole. Joint infection causes swelling, fibrin and cartilage damage. Clean and examine all feet, and open joints or collect deep samples only with veterinary guidance.
diseases.treatment: Treat the specific lesion: trim carefully, relieve pressure, clean and dress the foot, and provide pain relief. Use antibiotics only for bacterial infection under veterinary direction. Chronically affected cows may need culling; isolate infectious cases.
diseases.prevention: Use regular professional hoof trimming, clean dry standing areas, comfortable bedding and reduced standing time. Footbath where appropriate, manage slurry and heat stress, and feed a balanced ration that avoids rumen acidosis.

summary.en: A contagious fungal skin infection, common in young housed cattle. It causes circular scaly patches and can spread to people.
summary.ku: نەخۆشییەکی قارچیی گوازرەوەی پێستە، زۆر باوە لە گوێرە گەنجەکانی ناو حەوشە. پەڵەی خڕی قەلەفدار دروست دەکات و دەتوانێت بۆ مرۆڤ بگوازرێتەوە.
summary.ar: عدوى فطرية معدية للجلد، شائعة في العجول الصغيرة المحبوسة. تسبب بقعاً دائرية متقشرة ويمكن أن تنتقل إلى الإنسان.

diseases.zoonoticNote: Yes. Ringworm can spread from cattle to people through direct contact. Wear gloves, wash hands and avoid sharing brushes; children and immunosuppressed people should avoid handling affected animals.
diseases.notifiableNote: Not notifiable.
diseases.meatNote: Ringworm is a localized skin fungal infection; muscle from recovered or inspected cattle is safe for consumption.
diseases.causativeAgent: Dermatophyte fungi, especially Trichophyton verrucosum. Spores persist in hair, scabs, housing and equipment for long periods.
diseases.affected: Cattle of all ages, most often young stock and winter-housed animals. Malnourished or crowded cattle may be more severely affected. Sheep and people can also be infected.
symptoms: Circular, grey-white, scaly skin patches with hair loss
Raised or crusty margins; sometimes a red centre
Lesions on the head, neck, back, shoulders and around the eyes
Usually not very itchy, but may become secondarily infected
Clusters of cases in young stock after housing
diseases.diagnosis: The appearance is often typical, but skin scrapings, hair samples and fungal culture are useful for confusing cases. Ultraviolet Wood's lamp examination does not reliably confirm T. verrucosum. Check people with lesions through a doctor.
diseases.postMortem: Circular, grey-white crusty plaques with hair loss, mainly on the head, neck and back; the underlying skin may be thickened and inflamed. Lesions can be subtle or widespread, especially in calves. Microscopy of plucked hairs or skin scrapings and fungal culture confirm dermatophytes. Wear gloves because ringworm can affect people.
diseases.treatment: Many cattle recover over weeks to months. Topical antifungal washes, sprays or creams can help, while severe or spreading cases may need systemic treatment under veterinary direction. Treat secondary infection and do not use human medicines without advice.
diseases.prevention: Reduce overcrowding and improve ventilation, sunlight and hygiene. Clean and disinfect housing and equipment, do not share brushes, and isolate affected animals where practical. Vaccination is available in some countries. Hand hygiene prevents human infection.

summary.en: The fetal membranes are not expelled after calving, increasing the risk of uterine infection, poor milk yield and reduced fertility.
summary.ku: پلاسێنتا دوای سکاندن دەرنەچووە، ئەمە مەترسیی هەوکردنی ڕەحم، کەمبوونی شیر و کەمی زاوزێ زیاد دەکات.
summary.ar: لا تُطرد المشيمة بعد الولادة، مما يزيد خطر عدوى الرحم وقلة الحليب وانخفاض الخصوبة.

diseases.zoonoticNote: Not directly zoonotic, but the placenta may carry Brucella, Listeria or other pathogens. Wear gloves and wash thoroughly after handling.
diseases.notifiableNote: Not notifiable itself, but an abortion or retained placenta may trigger testing for brucellosis or other reportable diseases under herd rules.
diseases.meatNote: Meat is safe after full recovery and drug withdrawal. Animals suffering from acute septic metritis or systemic fever are condemned.
diseases.causativeAgent: Failure of placental separation and expulsion after birth. Risk factors include difficult calving, twins, caesarean section, induced calving, uterine inertia, heat stress and deficiencies of selenium, vitamin E or iodine. Brucellosis can also cause it.
diseases.affected: Cows are most commonly affected; ewes and goats can also retain membranes. Risk is higher after a difficult birth, twins, stillbirth or concurrent disease.
symptoms: Foul-smelling, dark membranes hanging from the vulva
Fever and reduced appetite when metritis develops
Reduced milk yield and depression
Straining and reddish-brown vaginal discharge
A closed cervix with membranes retained inside, sometimes with few visible signs
diseases.diagnosis: Confirm that membranes remain after 12–24 hours and assess the cow's temperature, hydration and uterine discharge. Check for metritis and underlying disease. Brucellosis testing may be required depending on herd and country rules.
diseases.postMortem: Foetal membranes remain hanging from the vulva beyond the expected time, and the uterus may be atonic and contaminated. Metritis can produce a thickened, inflamed endometrium with purulent exudate. Check for twins, abortion and systemic illness. Submit placenta and uterine swabs for culture when metritis or abortion is suspected.
diseases.treatment: Do not forcibly pull the membranes, as this can damage the uterus. Encourage self-clearance and provide veterinary care for fever, pain or uterine infection. Antibiotics are used only when indicated. Surgery or specialist care may be needed if the cervix closes.
diseases.prevention: Provide balanced transition nutrition, hygienic calving facilities and prompt assistance for difficult births. Monitor cows after twins or dystocia, control brucellosis and avoid overconditioning. Record cases to identify herd-level problems.

summary.en: A painful bacterial infection of the foot that spreads in warm, muddy conditions, causing severe lameness and weight loss.
summary.ku: هەوکردنێکی باکتریایی ئازاردەری پێیە کە لە کەشوهەوای گەرم و قوڕاویدا بڵاو دەبێتەوە و لەنگبوونی توند و کەمبوونی کێش دروست دەکات.
summary.ar: عدوى بكتيرية مؤلمة للقدم تنتشر في الظروف الدافئة والطينية، وتسبب عرجاً شديداً وفقدان الوزن.

diseases.zoonoticNote: Not a zoonosis. Use gloves when treating feet because manure bacteria can infect skin wounds.
diseases.notifiableNote: Not usually notifiable, but some countries regulate virulent foot rot in eradication programmes.
diseases.meatNote: Meat is safe after routine trimming of affected feet and post-mortem inspection, provided no active systemic fever or drug residues exist.
diseases.causativeAgent: Dichelobacter nodosus is the essential pathogen, often acting with Fusobacterium necrophorum. The bacteria survive in hoof tissue and wet soil; moisture and mud are major risk factors.
diseases.affected: Sheep of all ages, especially adults in wet, muddy conditions or overcrowded pens. Unvaccinated flocks and animals with chronically affected feet are important sources.
symptoms: Lameness, often severe and sudden
Foul-smelling, moist necrosis between the claws
Separation of the hoof horn from underlying tissue
Reluctance to walk, graze or stand for shearing
Weight loss and reduced wool growth
diseases.diagnosis: Inspect the feet in clean, dry conditions and look for characteristic smell and undermined hoof horn. Differentiate from foot abscess, foot scald and contagious ovine digital dermatitis. Laboratory culture can confirm virulent strains.
diseases.postMortem: Erosive, necrotic lesions of the interdigital skin and deeper tissues, often with a foul smell; hoof horn may separate in chronic cases. Tendons and joints can become involved in severe disease. Clean and examine all feet, and rule out foot abscess, contagious ovine digital dermatitis and foot-and-mouth disease. Culture affected tissue for Dichelobacter nodosus and Fusobacterium necrophorum.
diseases.treatment: Trim exposed horn carefully, clean and dry the foot and apply an approved topical treatment or footbath under veterinary direction. Severe cases may need parenteral antibiotics; observe withdrawal periods. Isolate and treat lame sheep early.
diseases.prevention: Keep standing areas dry, footbath strategically, avoid muddy overcrowding and quarantine purchased sheep for inspection. Vaccination may help where available and appropriate. Cull animals with repeated chronic infection.

summary.en: A clostridial disease triggered by sudden rich feed, causing rapid toxin production and often sudden death in fast-growing lambs.
summary.ku: نەخۆشییەکی کلۆستریدیالییە کە بە خۆراکی دەوڵەمەندی لەناکاو دەست پێدەکات و دروستکردنی خێرای ژەهر و زۆرجار مردنی لەناکاوی گوێرەی گەشەسەندوو دروست دەکات.
summary.ar: مرض كلوستريدي يحفزه العلف الغني المفاجئ، ويسبب إنتاجاً سريعاً للسموم وغالباً موتاً مفاجئاً في الحملان سريعة النمو.

diseases.zoonoticNote: Not a zoonosis.
diseases.notifiableNote: Not notifiable.
diseases.meatNote: Animals dying of enterotoxaemia are unfit for consumption; toxin-laden tissues and dead animals must never enter the food chain.
diseases.causativeAgent: Clostridium perfringens type D multiplies rapidly when rich feed or lush pasture passes into the intestine. It releases epsilon toxin, which damages the gut, kidneys and brain.
diseases.affected: Sheep, especially rapidly growing lambs, feedlot lambs and recently weaned animals. Adults on lush pasture or suddenly increased grain can also die.
symptoms: Sudden death, often without warning
Collapse, paddling or convulsions shortly before death
Colic and diarrhoea
Stiffness, incoordination and head posture changes
Post-mortem evidence of soft kidneys and fluid around the heart
diseases.diagnosis: Diagnosis is often made at post-mortem with compatible signs, history of a sudden feed change and detection of type D toxin in intestinal contents. Urgent samples should be collected by a veterinarian.
diseases.postMortem: The carcass decomposes rapidly and is often found dead; serous or haemorrhagic fluid may be present in the pericardium, pleura and peritoneum. The small intestine can be congested and oedematous, and the kidneys are soft and pulpy, although this change is not always present. Brain oedema and haemorrhage may occur. Confirm epsilon toxin in intestinal contents and rule out anthrax before opening the carcass.
diseases.treatment: Treatment is usually too late because death occurs quickly. Early cases require immediate veterinary care with antitoxin, antibiotics and supportive fluid therapy where appropriate. Do not attempt home remedies.
diseases.prevention: Vaccinate ewes before lambing and lambs according to the vaccine label. Introduce grain and rich pasture gradually, avoid sudden overeating and provide adequate fibre. Ensure lambs receive good colostrum.

summary.en: A severe, highly contagious viral disease of sheep and goats causing fever, mouth lesions, diarrhoea and pneumonia. It is a major livestock and trade threat.
summary.ku: نەخۆشییەکی ڤایرۆسی توند و زۆر گوازرەوەیە لە مەڕ و بزن؛ تا، برینی دەم، سکچوون و سیەسۆیل دروست دەکات. مەترسییەکی گەورەیە بۆ ئاژەڵداری و بازرگانی.
summary.ar: مرض فيروسي شديد وشديد العدوى يصيب الأغنام والماعز ويسبب الحمى وتقرحات الفم والإسهال والالتهاب الرئوي. ويمثل تهديداً كبيراً للثروة الحيوانية والتجارة.

diseases.zoonoticNote: PPR is not known to infect humans. Normal hygiene is still important when handling sick animals.
diseases.notifiableNote: WOAH-listed and reportable in nearly all countries. Suspected cases must be reported immediately; do not move animals or samples without official advice.
diseases.meatNote: PPR is a severe notifiable viral disease; affected animals are subject to official slaughter, quarantine, and carcass destruction.
diseases.causativeAgent: Peste des petits ruminants virus, a morbillivirus in the family Paramyxoviridae. It spreads by close contact, respiratory secretions, faeces and contaminated equipment.
diseases.affected: Sheep and goats of all ages, with high morbidity and mortality in naive flocks. Goats may be particularly severely affected; cattle are not affected.
symptoms: High fever and sudden depression
Nose and eye discharge; crusty muzzle
Mouth erosions, foul breath and drooling
Cough, rapid breathing and pneumonia
Profuse diarrhoea, dehydration and weight loss
Abortion in some pregnant animals; death in severe outbreaks
diseases.diagnosis: Confirm with PCR or antigen detection on swabs, blood, lymph node or tissue samples, and use serology for surveillance. Immediate reporting is mandatory. Differentiate from bluetongue, sheep pox, orf and pneumonia.
diseases.postMortem: Erosive stomatitis, pharyngitis and enteritis; the tongue, gums and hard palate may show necrosis. Congestion and haemorrhage in the intestines and enlarged lymph nodes are common. The lungs may show interstitial pneumonia and the spleen is often small. PPR is notifiable; collect samples through official channels with full biosecurity.
diseases.treatment: There is no specific antiviral treatment. Provide supportive fluids, soft feed and nursing care; antibiotics may be used only for secondary bacterial infection under veterinary direction. Official outbreak control may include vaccination and culling.
diseases.prevention: Vaccination is the main control tool, supported by quarantine, movement restrictions, surveillance and safe disposal of carcasses. Global eradication relies on high vaccination coverage and rapid reporting of disease.

summary.en: A contagious poxvirus disease causing fever and widespread skin pustules and scabs, especially around the face, mouth and udder.
summary.ku: نەخۆشییەکی ڤایرۆسی پۆکسە و گوازرەوەیە؛ تا و پەپولەی پێست و قەلەف دروست دەکات، بەتایبەتی لە دەموچاو، دەم و مەمک.
summary.ar: مرض فيروسي معدي من مجموعة الجدري يسبب الحمى وبثوراً وقشوراً جلدية منتشرة، خاصة حول الوجه والفم والضرع.

diseases.zoonoticNote: Sheep pox is not known to infect humans. Wear gloves for skin lesions to prevent secondary bacterial infection.
diseases.notifiableNote: WOAH-listed and reportable in many countries. Report suspicion and apply movement restrictions immediately.
diseases.meatNote: Sheep pox is a reportable disease causing systemic lesions; carcasses of affected sheep are condemned under official regulations.
diseases.causativeAgent: Sheep pox virus, a capripoxvirus. It spreads by direct contact, contaminated equipment, insects and perhaps aerosol in close groups. The virus survives in scabs.
diseases.affected: Sheep of all ages; young lambs and naive flocks can be severely affected. Some sheep breeds appear more resistant.
symptoms: High fever and nasal or eye discharge
Red spots that become papules and pustules on the face, lips, udder and scrotum
Crusts, ulcers and secondary skin infection
Reduced appetite, weight loss and a drop in milk
Abortion or death in severe cases
Lambs may die rapidly without obvious extensive skin lesions
diseases.diagnosis: Confirm with PCR on skin lesions, scabs or blood, or virus isolation in a reference laboratory. Differentiate from orf, bluetongue and PPR. Notify authorities before moving samples.
diseases.postMortem: Firm, raised skin nodules, especially on the face, ears, udder and perineum, progress from vesicles and pustules to crusts. Similar lesions may occur in the mouth, pharynx, trachea and lungs, and lymph nodes are enlarged. Severe cases develop pneumonia and secondary infection. Sheep pox is notifiable in many countries; submit skin and lymph node samples for PCR through official channels.
diseases.treatment: No specific antiviral treatment. Provide soft feed, fluids and nursing care, and control secondary bacterial infection and fly strike under veterinary advice. Isolate affected animals and dispose of contaminated material safely.
diseases.prevention: Vaccinate with an approved vaccine where available and permitted, quarantine new sheep and control insects and fomites. Follow official movement restrictions and report all suspected cases.

summary.en: A fatal prion disease of sheep affecting the brain. There is no treatment, and control depends on flock genetics, surveillance and biosecurity.
summary.ku: نەخۆشییەکی پرایۆنی کوشندەیە کە دەماری مەڕ تووش دەکات. چارەسەر نییە؛ کۆنترۆڵ بەپێی بۆماوەی گەلە، چاودێری و بایۆسکیورییتی دەبێت.
summary.ar: مرض بريوني قاتل يصيب دماغ الأغنام. لا يوجد علاج، وتعتمد المكافحة على وراثة القطيع والمراقبة والأمن الحيوي.

diseases.zoonoticNote: Scrapie is not considered a human zoonosis. Prion diseases require special handling, so follow national rules for carcasses and laboratory samples.
diseases.notifiableNote: Usually notifiable and subject to national surveillance and eradication programmes. Do not move animals or dispose of carcasses outside official advice.
diseases.meatNote: Scrapie is a reportable transmissible spongiform encephalopathy; carcasses and specified risk materials are strictly excluded from the food chain.
diseases.causativeAgent: Misfolded prion proteins accumulate in the brain and lymphoid tissue. Infection spreads within flocks, especially around lambing and through contaminated pasture, pens and equipment.
diseases.affected: Sheep, usually adults 2–5 years old; goats can also be affected. Susceptibility is strongly influenced by prion-protein genotype and breed.
symptoms: Progressive scratching, rubbing and wool loss
Behaviour change, nervousness or aggression
Tremors, incoordination and unusual head movements
Lip smacking and abnormal gait
Weight loss despite a normal appetite
Eventually recumbency and death; fever is absent
diseases.diagnosis: There is no reliable live diagnostic test. Confirmation requires post-mortem brain examination using Western blot or immunohistochemistry, together with national genotype testing. Report suspected cases before tissue collection.
diseases.postMortem: There are often no gross lesions; emaciation and poor fleece may be the only findings. Histopathology of the brain and spinal cord shows spongiform change, neuronal vacuolation and astrogliosis, and abnormal prion protein can be detected by immunohistochemistry or Western blot. Scrapie is a reportable transmissible spongiform encephalopathy in many countries; do not perform a home necropsy without official advice.
diseases.treatment: There is no treatment, and the disease is progressive and fatal. Euthanasia is appropriate for welfare and disease control, under official guidance. Do not attempt unapproved treatments.
diseases.prevention: Breed for scrapie-resistant genotypes, source sheep from flocks with known status and maintain lambing/pen hygiene. Follow national surveillance, culling and movement rules. Do not feed ruminant-derived protein to ruminants.

summary.en: A bacterial infection of sheep, especially rams, causing swollen testicles and poor breeding performance. Ewes may abort or produce weak lambs.
summary.ku: نەخۆشییەکی باکتریایی مەڕە، بەتایبەتی بەران؛ ئاوسانی گون و کەمی توانای زاوزێ دروست دەکات. مەڕەکان لەوانەیە سکێنن یان بەرەبچووی لاواز لەدایک بێنن.
summary.ar: عدوى بكتيرية تصيب الأغنام وخاصة الكباش، وتسبب تورم الخصية وضعف الأداء التناسلي. قد تجهض النعاج أو تلد حملاناً ضعيفة.

diseases.zoonoticNote: B. ovis is not considered a significant human pathogen, but sheep can also carry B. melitensis. Use gloves and seek advice before handling abortion material.
diseases.notifiableNote: Reportable in many countries, particularly for trade and breeding controls. National rules vary; check with the local veterinary authority.
diseases.meatNote: Infected animals are subject to official flock disease control and rejection at slaughter inspection.
diseases.causativeAgent: Brucella ovis, a bacterium spread mainly by venereal contact and direct contact between rams. Infected rams can remain carriers and shed bacteria in semen.
diseases.affected: Sheep, especially sexually mature rams. Ewes can be infected and may abort, but often show no clear signs. The disease reduces flock lambing rates.
symptoms: Swollen, painful epididymis or scrotum in rams
Poor semen quality and reduced fertility
Abortion, stillbirth or weak lambs in ewes
Reduced lambing percentage across the flock
Often no obvious signs in infected ewes
diseases.diagnosis: Use serology in rams and ewes, supported by culture or PCR on semen, placenta or abortion material. Rams should have a breeding soundness examination. Work with the veterinary authority on official testing.
diseases.postMortem: Rams show epididymitis with enlarged, firm or asymmetrical testes and thickened scrotal skin; the epididymis may contain caseous or purulent material. Ewes may abort or retain the placenta, although signs are often mild. Regional lymph nodes can be enlarged. Handle reproductive tissues with gloves and official biosecurity because brucellosis is zoonotic.
diseases.treatment: There is no practical treatment for breeding flocks. Identify and cull infected rams, control mating and test replacement animals. People handling abortion material should use protective clothing even though B. ovis is not the main human risk.
diseases.prevention: Buy rams from tested flocks, avoid mixing breeding rams and use single-sire mating where possible. Test rams before the breeding season, cull reactors and follow national brucellosis control rules. Quarantine all new stock.

summary.en: A contagious poxvirus infection causing scabby sores on the mouth and muzzle, particularly in lambs. It can spread to people handling affected animals.
summary.ku: نەخۆشییەکی ڤایرۆسی پۆکسە و گوازرەوەیە کە قەلەفی برینی دەم و لووت دروست دەکات، بەتایبەتی لە بەرخان. دەتوانێت بۆ مرۆڤی سەرقاڵی ئاژەڵەکانیش بگوازرێتەوە.
summary.ar: عدوى فيروسية معدية من مجموعة الجدري تسبب قروحاً متقشرة حول الفم والخطم، خاصة في الحملان. يمكن أن تنتقل إلى الإنسان عند التعامل مع الحيوانات المصابة.

diseases.zoonoticNote: Yes. Orf causes painful finger or hand lesions in people. Wear gloves, cover cuts and wash hands. Immunosuppressed people should avoid contact; human lesions need medical advice.
diseases.notifiableNote: Not usually notifiable.
diseases.meatNote: Orf is a contagious zoonotic virus; handling active lesions carries infection risk and affected tissue or carcasses are rejected under inspection.
diseases.causativeAgent: Orf virus, a parapoxvirus. It survives in scabs and on contaminated equipment, so infection can spread long after the animal has recovered.
diseases.affected: Sheep and goats of all ages; lambs and unvaccinated flocks are most affected. People handling affected animals, especially during lambing, are at risk.
symptoms: Proliferative, scabby sores around the lips, muzzle and nostrils
Lesions on the teats and feet in some animals
Reluctance to suck or eat, leading to poor growth
Secondary bacterial infection, fly strike or mastitis
Lesions usually heal over several weeks
diseases.diagnosis: The appearance is usually characteristic. PCR or electron microscopy can confirm unusual cases. Wear gloves during examination. Human lesions are diagnosed by a doctor and often follow animal contact.
diseases.postMortem: Proliferative, crusty and sometimes pustular lesions on the lips, muzzle, eyelids, udder and feet. Lesions can extend into the mouth and pharynx, especially in young lambs. Secondary bacterial infection may cause deeper necrosis. Orf is zoonotic; wear gloves and submit scabs or fresh tissue for PCR or electron microscopy.
diseases.treatment: No specific antiviral is available. Clean lesions with an approved antiseptic, control secondary bacteria and flies, and provide soft feed. Vaccination during an outbreak is controversial and may not prevent infection; consult a veterinarian.
diseases.prevention: Vaccinate before lambing or high-risk periods where approved. Avoid rough feed that injures mouths, disinfect equipment and isolate affected animals. Wear gloves, dispose of scabs safely and maintain strict hand hygiene.

summary.en: A serious metabolic disease in late pregnancy, usually in ewes carrying multiple lambs. Inadequate energy intake leads to ketone build-up and brain signs.
summary.ku: نەخۆشییەکی میتابۆلیکی مەترسیدارە لە کۆتایی دووگیانیدا، زۆرجار لە مەڕی دوو یان زیاتر برخ. کەمی وزەی وەرگیراو دەبێتە هۆی کۆبوونەوەی کیتۆن و نیشانەی دەماری.
summary.ar: مرض أيضي خطير في أواخر الحمل، غالباً في النعاج الحاملة لعدة حملان. قلة الطاقة المتناولة تؤدي إلى تراكم الكيتونات وعلامات عصبية.

diseases.zoonoticNote: Not a zoonosis.
diseases.notifiableNote: Not notifiable.
diseases.meatNote: Ewes affected by severe pregnancy toxaemia are hypoglycaemic, emaciated, and unfit for meat consumption.
diseases.causativeAgent: Negative energy balance in late gestation. Multiple lambs, obesity, poor feed intake, stress, cold weather and dental problems increase energy demand and fat mobilisation.
diseases.affected: Pregnant ewes, especially in the last 4–6 weeks before lambing and those carrying twins or triplets. Thin or overfat ewes and ewes with reduced appetite are at risk.
symptoms: Dullness, separation from the flock and reduced appetite
Sweet or acetone-like breath and ketones in urine
Weakness, tremors and an unsteady gait
Recumbency, head pressing, blindness or convulsions
Dehydration and death near lambing if untreated
diseases.diagnosis: Use the history, ketone testing on urine or blood and clinical signs. Measure blood glucose and electrolytes where possible. Assess fetal viability and look for hypocalcaemia or concurrent disease.
diseases.postMortem: The ewe is often emaciated with a large twin or triplet pregnancy, a pale fatty liver and an underfilled rumen. Dehydration and a ketone smell may be present, and the uterus may contain autolysed foetuses. Check for hypocalcaemia, mastitis and concurrent disease; liver and blood samples can support the diagnosis.
diseases.treatment: Urgent veterinary care is needed. Provide oral propylene glycol or glucose as directed and intravenous fluids/glucose for severe cases. Relieve energy demand by delivering lambs if the ewe is near term and the veterinarian advises. Provide pain relief and nursing.
diseases.prevention: Condition-score ewes at mating and late pregnancy, scan for multiple lambs and feed a balanced, palatable late-pregnancy ration. Avoid obesity and sudden feed restriction, monitor intake, and manage cold stress and concurrent disease.

summary.en: A chronic bacterial disease causing abscesses in lymph nodes and internal organs. Thick cheesy pus can spread infection through flocks.
summary.ku: نەخۆشییەکی باکتریایی درێژخایەنە کە ئێسکی پڕ لە زوو لە گرێی لیمفاوی و ئەندامانی ناوەوە دروست دەکات. زووی چەسپاو تووشبوون بڵاو دەکاتەوە.
summary.ar: مرض بكتيري مزمن يسبب خراجات في العقد اللمفاوية والأعضاء الداخلية. القيح السميك الجبني ينشر العدوى بين القطيع.

diseases.zoonoticNote: Rare human infection can occur through contact with pus or contaminated equipment. Wear gloves and eye protection when draining abscesses or handling carcasses.
diseases.notifiableNote: Not usually notifiable, though region-specific control programmes may require reporting.
diseases.meatNote: CLA causes visceral and lymph node abscesses; affected carcasses undergo extensive trimming or full condemnation at meat inspection.
diseases.causativeAgent: Corynebacterium pseudotuberculosis. The bacteria survive in pus and on shearing equipment, and enter through skin wounds or the respiratory tract.
diseases.affected: Sheep and goats; adults in intensive flocks are most commonly affected. Young stock can be infected through contaminated shearing or close contact.
symptoms: Recurrent abscesses in lymph nodes, often under the jaw or on the shoulder
Thick, green-white, cheesy pus; abscesses may rupture
Weight loss and poor wool growth
Internal abscesses in the lungs and liver, causing chronic ill thrift
Reduced milk yield and occasional respiratory signs
diseases.diagnosis: Culture or PCR of pus, or post-mortem examination of internal abscesses. Serology can help screen flocks but is imperfect. Distinguish from tuberculosis and other causes of lymph-node swelling.
diseases.postMortem: Enlarged lymph nodes, especially superficial nodes of the head, neck and shoulder, contain thick greenish-yellow caseous pus with a laminated onion-ring appearance. Similar abscesses may occur in the lungs, liver, spleen, kidneys and udder. The pus is often inspissated and surrounded by a fibrous capsule. Culture or PCR of pus confirms Corynebacterium pseudotuberculosis.
diseases.treatment: Individual abscesses may be drained by a veterinarian with strict hygiene; antibiotics are often disappointing once abscesses form. Cull chronically affected animals. Always dispose of pus and contaminated bedding safely.
diseases.prevention: Use a vaccine where available, keep shearing equipment clean and disinfected, avoid overcrowding and isolate animals with draining abscesses. Cull recurrent cases and maintain closed-flock biosecurity where possible.

summary.en: A blood-feeding stomach worm that causes anaemia, bottle jaw and weight loss. Heavy infections can kill sheep quickly, especially in warm, wet seasons.
summary.ku: کرمێکی گەدەیە کە خوێن دەخوات و کەمی خوێن، ئاوسانی ژێر شەویلگە و کەمبوونی کێش دروست دەکات. تووشبوونی زۆر دەتوانێت بە خێرایی مەڕ بکوژێت، بەتایبەتی لە وەرزی گەرم و شێدار.
summary.ar: دودة معوية تتغذى على الدم وتسبب فقر الدم وتورم تحت الفك وفقدان الوزن. الإصابات الشديدة قد تقتل الأغنام بسرعة، خاصة في المواسم الدافئة الرطبة.

diseases.zoonoticNote: Not a zoonosis.
diseases.notifiableNote: Not notifiable.
diseases.meatNote: Severe haemonchosis causes extreme anaemia and watery muscle, leading to condemnation at slaughter inspection.
diseases.causativeAgent: Haemonchus contortus, a blood-feeding nematode in the abomasum. Warm, moist conditions and high stocking density increase pasture contamination and larvae availability.
diseases.affected: Sheep, especially young stock, lactating ewes and naive animals. Goats are also affected. Adults may tolerate infection while continuing to contaminate pasture.
symptoms: Progressive weight loss and poor growth
Pale gums and eyelids from anaemia
Bottle-jaw swelling under the jaw
Weakness and reduced exercise tolerance
Diarrhoea or soft faeces
Sudden death in heavy infections, sometimes before obvious wasting
diseases.diagnosis: Use faecal egg counts with larval culture or PCR to identify species, and apply a FAMACHA-style anaemia score to individuals. Monitor faecal egg count reduction after treatment to detect resistance.
diseases.postMortem: The carcass is pale and anaemic with watery blood. The abomasum contains brownish fluid and many slender Haemonchus contortus worms, and its mucosa is congested and oedematous. Black tarry faeces may be present in the gut, and the liver and spleen may be small. Faecal egg counts and post-mortem worm counts confirm the burden.
diseases.treatment: Select a dewormer with veterinary advice based on faecal results, drench by accurate body weight and follow local resistance guidelines. Treat severe anaemia supportively; blood transfusion is rarely available but may help. Do not treat all sheep automatically.
diseases.prevention: Use rotational grazing and rest periods, avoid overstocking, maintain good nutrition and use targeted selective treatment based on anaemia and faecal counts. Quarantine new sheep, test for resistant worms and reduce reliance on a single drug family.

summary.en: A protozoal gut infection, mostly in young lambs, causing diarrhoea, poor growth and dehydration. Crowded, dirty conditions increase risk.
summary.ku: نەخۆشییەکی پڕۆتۆزۆیی ڕیخۆڵەیە، زۆرجار لە بەرخانی گەنجدا؛ سکچوون، کەمگەشە و وشکبوون دروست دەکات. قەرەباڵغی و پیسی مەترسی زیاد دەکەن.
summary.ar: عدوى طفيلية في الأمعاء تصيب الحملان الصغيرة غالباً، وتسبب الإسهال وضعف النمو والجفاف. الازدحام والنظافة السيئة يزيدان الخطر.

diseases.zoonoticNote: Sheep Eimeria species are host-specific and not transmitted to people.
diseases.notifiableNote: Not notifiable.
diseases.meatNote: Acute coccidiosis causes emaciation and severe enteritis; affected lambs showing systemic signs are condemned.
diseases.causativeAgent: Eimeria species, especially in young lambs after exposure to contaminated bedding or pasture. Oocysts survive well in damp, dirty environments.
diseases.affected: Lambs, especially around 2–8 weeks after first exposure and after weaning. Overcrowded, stressed or recently moved lambs are at highest risk. Adults usually develop immunity.
symptoms: Watery or blood-stained diarrhoea
Abdominal pain and straining
Reduced appetite and growth
Dehydration and weakness
Losses in untreated outbreaks; poor performance after recovery
diseases.diagnosis: Faecal oocyst counts and species identification, interpreted with the lamb's age and clinical signs. Bloody diarrhoea can also be caused by enterotoxaemia, salmonellosis or worms, so a veterinary examination is required.
diseases.postMortem: The small or large intestine is thickened, congested and sometimes haemorrhagic, with white or yellow caseous plaques and blood-stained contents. Lesions are often most severe in the ileum, caecum and colon, and mesenteric lymph nodes may be enlarged. Microscopy of mucosal scrapings shows coccidial oocysts and life stages. Rule out other causes of diarrhoea.
