diseases.treatment: Use an appropriate anticoccidial under veterinary advice and provide oral or intravenous fluids for dehydration. Support nutrition and isolate severely affected lambs. Avoid treating without a diagnosis in an outbreak.
diseases.prevention: Keep bedding clean and dry, reduce overcrowding, separate age groups and rotate pastures. Use coccidiostats in feed or water where licensed, and minimise weaning and transport stress. Investigate repeated outbreaks.

summary.en: Udder infection in ewes reduces milk supply and can leave lambs hungry. Severe cases can progress to gangrene or death.
summary.ku: هەوکردنی مەمک لە مەڕدا شیر کەم دەکات و دەتوانێت بەرخان برسی بکات. حاڵەتە توندەکان دەتوانن بۆ گرانگرین یان مردن بگەن.
summary.ar: عدوى الضرع في النعاج تقلل إنتاج الحليب وقد تترك الحملان جائعة. الحالات الشديدة قد تتطور إلى غرغرينا أو موت.

diseases.zoonoticNote: Not usually zoonotic, but milk from affected ewes should not enter the food chain until veterinary advice and withdrawal periods are respected.
diseases.notifiableNote: Not notifiable.
diseases.meatNote: Meat from fully recovered ewes is safe after official meat inspection and full compliance with drug withdrawal periods.
diseases.causativeAgent: Staphylococcus aureus, coagulase-negative staphylococci, Mannheimia haemolytica and Streptococcus species. Poor udder conformation, dirty bedding and low body condition increase risk.
diseases.affected: Lactating ewes and ewes around lambing, especially those with poor nutrition, multiple lambs or udder injury. Chronic cases may be culled.
symptoms: A hot, swollen and painful udder, often one-sided
Watery, blood-stained, clotted or purulent milk
Hungry, restless lambs despite a full-looking udder
Fever, reduced appetite and depression
Dark, cold udder skin or collapse in severe staphylococcal cases
diseases.diagnosis: Examine both halves of the udder and strip milk onto a clean strip cup. Culture and sensitivity can guide antibiotic choice. Check that lambs are receiving enough milk and look for concurrent disease.
diseases.postMortem: The affected udder is hot, swollen and painful, with watery, clotted or blood-stained milk; abscesses and gangrene can occur in severe cases. Supramammary lymph nodes are enlarged. Chronic mastitis leaves the gland firm and fibrotic. Culture of milk or gland tissue identifies the pathogen; necropsy is mainly used in fatal or chronic flock cases.
diseases.treatment: Provide pain relief, fluids and supportive care, strip the affected side regularly and use an appropriate antibiotic under veterinary direction. Feed lambs artificially if the ewe cannot nurse. Severe gangrenous mastitis may require euthanasia.
diseases.prevention: Ensure good ewe nutrition and condition, provide clean dry lambing areas, check udders after lambing and control flies. Cull ewes with chronic udder damage and avoid overcrowding. Treat teat injuries early.

summary.en: A mite infestation that causes intense itching, wool loss and crusted skin. Sheep scab is highly contagious and reportable in some areas.
summary.ku: تووشبوون بە مایتە کە خۆریدانی توند، ڕژانی خوری و پێستی قەلەفدار دروست دەکات. گەریی مەڕ زۆر گوازرەوەیە و لە هەندێک ناوچەدا پێویستە ڕاپۆرت بکرێت.
summary.ar: إصابة بالقمل أو العث تسبب حكة شديدة وتساقط الصوف وقشوراً جلدية. جرب الأغنام شديد العدوى ويجب الإبلاغ عنه في بعض المناطق.

diseases.zoonoticNote: Sheep scab mites are not human parasites, but some other mange mites can cause temporary itchy skin in people. Wear gloves and wash clothing.
diseases.notifiableNote: Sheep scab is notifiable in some countries for control programmes. Report suspected cases and follow local movement and treatment rules.
diseases.meatNote: Sheep scab is a reportable infestation; heavily infested or treated sheep cannot be slaughtered until official clearance and withdrawal times pass.
diseases.causativeAgent: Psoroptes ovis mites cause sheep scab; Sarcoptes and Chorioptes mites can also cause mange. Mites spread by direct contact and contaminated equipment, and survive away from the host for a limited time.
diseases.affected: Sheep of all ages, especially in winter and in untreated flocks. Introduced animals and animals in poor condition are common sources.
symptoms: Intense itching; rubbing, biting and stamping
Wool loss, especially over the neck, back and flanks
Crusted, inflamed, exudative skin
Restlessness and poor weight gain
Secondary bacterial infection; rapid spread through a group
diseases.diagnosis: Take skin scrapings from the edge of lesions and identify mites under a microscope. Serology for Psoroptes may be available. Inspect all in-contact sheep because early cases can be missed.
diseases.postMortem: The skin is thickened, crusty and inflamed with hair loss, especially around the face, ears, shoulders and flanks; folds and exudate may develop. Deep skin scrapings show Psoroptes mites. Sheep scab is reportable in many countries, so use gloves and submit samples through official channels. Secondary bacterial infection can complicate the lesions.
diseases.treatment: Treat all in-contact sheep with an approved acaricide, using the correct product, dose and interval. Isolate affected animals and clean equipment and trailers. Some products have long meat and milk withdrawal periods.
diseases.prevention: Quarantine and inspect all introduced sheep, treat entire groups at the same time, disinfect equipment and avoid sharing trailers or shearing gear. Monitor in winter and follow national sheep-scab controls.

summary.en: Blowfly larvae infest soiled fleece or wounds, causing painful skin damage and potentially fatal toxaemia. Humid weather raises the risk.
summary.ku: کرمی مێش لە خوری پیس یان برینەکاندا جێگیر دەبێت، زیانی ئازاردەری پێست و ژەهرخواردنی کوشندە دروست دەکات. کەشوهەوای شێدار مەترسی زیاد دەکات.
summary.ar: تغزو يرقات الذباب الصوف الملوث أو الجروح، مسببة تلفاً جلدياً مؤلماً وتسمماً دموياً قد يكون قاتلاً. الطقس الرطب يرفع الخطر.

diseases.zoonoticNote: Not generally a zoonosis. Use gloves when removing maggots and cleaning wounds.
diseases.notifiableNote: Not notifiable.
diseases.meatNote: Fly strike causes severe tissue necrosis, bacterial infection, and toxaemia; affected sheep are unfit for human consumption.
diseases.causativeAgent: Blowfly species such as Lucilia cuprina lay eggs in soiled fleece, wounds or damaged skin. Larvae feed on tissue and release toxins. Diarrhoea, urine staining, fleece rot and warm damp weather are major triggers.
diseases.affected: Sheep of all ages, particularly unshorn adults with dirty breeches, wounds or chronic diarrhoea. Lambs can also be struck around the tail or navel.
symptoms: Restlessness, stamping and nibbling at the skin
Dirty, wet fleece with a foul smell
Visible maggots and painful raw skin
Reduced grazing and weight loss
Depression, toxaemia and death in severe cases
diseases.diagnosis: Part the fleece and inspect the skin for maggots, damaged tissue and moisture. Assess for dehydration and toxaemia. Identify the underlying cause, such as diarrhoea, dags or a wound.
diseases.postMortem: Foul-smelling, moist fleece with matted wool and visible maggots, usually around the tail, breech, feet or wounds. The underlying skin is inflamed, ulcerated and sometimes necrotic. Severe cases develop toxaemia and dehydration. Clip and examine the area carefully, record tissue damage, and look for underlying wounds or diarrhoea.
diseases.treatment: Remove affected wool and maggots, clip and clean the area, and apply an approved insecticide under veterinary direction. Treat pain and toxaemia; severely affected sheep may need euthanasia. Control the underlying cause.
diseases.prevention: Prevent dirty breeches by controlling worms and diarrhoea, maintain appropriate tail length and crutching, treat wounds promptly and use fly repellents or insect growth regulators. Check high-risk sheep daily in warm, humid weather.

summary.en: A midge-borne viral disease that can cause fever, swollen blue tongue, lameness and abortion in sheep. It is reportable and can severely affect flocks.
summary.ku: نەخۆشییەکی ڤایرۆسییە کە بە مێشۆکە دەگوازرێتەوە و دەتوانێت تا، زمانى ئاوساوی شین، لەنگبوون و سکاندن لە مەڕ دروست بکات. پێویستە ڕاپۆرت بکرێت.
summary.ar: مرض فيروسي ينتقل بالبعوض الصغير يسبب الحمى وتورم اللسان الأزرق والعرج والإجهاض في الأغنام. يجب الإبلاغ عنه وقد يؤثر بشدة على القطعان.

diseases.zoonoticNote: Bluetongue does not infect humans. Use standard hygiene when handling sick animals.
diseases.notifiableNote: WOAH-listed and reportable in most countries. Movement restrictions and vector controls may apply; report suspicion immediately.
diseases.meatNote: Bluetongue is a reportable viral disease causing systemic vascular damage; affected livestock are condemned at slaughter.
diseases.causativeAgent: Bluetongue virus, an orbivirus with multiple serotypes, transmitted by Culicoides biting midges. Cattle can carry virus and serve as a source for midges, even without severe signs.
diseases.affected: Sheep are often most severely affected, especially naive sheep moved into an endemic area. Cattle and other ruminants can be infected; goats usually show milder disease.
symptoms: High fever and depression
Swollen, blue or purple tongue and lips; drooling
Nasal discharge and ulcers around the mouth and nose
Lameness and foot lesions from swelling
Abortion, weak lambs and a milk drop
Death in severe sheep cases
diseases.diagnosis: Detect viral RNA by PCR on blood, spleen or lesions and determine the serotype. Report suspected cases officially before moving animals. Differentiate from FMD, PPR, sheep pox and orf.
diseases.postMortem: Congestion, oedema and haemorrhage of the muzzle, lips, tongue, gums and coronary bands, with ulcers in some cases. The lungs may be oedematous and the pericardium may contain fluid; the spleen can be enlarged. Lesions are often more severe in sheep than cattle. Bluetongue is notifiable; collect samples through official channels with insect-proof biosecurity.
diseases.treatment: There is no specific antiviral treatment. Provide supportive fluids, soft feed, nursing care, anti-inflammatory treatment and control of secondary infection as directed. Rest and good housing improve recovery.
diseases.prevention: Vaccinate against the locally circulating serotypes where licensed, reduce midge exposure with housing and screens, and follow official movement and vector-control measures. Report and quarantine suspected cases immediately.

summary.en: The same highly contagious virus that affects cattle can cause milder, easily missed signs in sheep. Prompt reporting is essential to protect other livestock.
summary.ku: هەمان ڤایرۆسی زۆر گوازرەوەی مانگا دەتوانێت نیشانەی سووک و ئاسان لەدەستچوو لە مەڕ دروست بکات. ڕاپۆرتکردنی خێرا بۆ پاراستنی ئاژەڵانی دیکە پێویستە.
summary.ar: نفس الفيروس شديد العدوى الذي يصيب الأبقار قد يسبب علامات أخف ويصعب ملاحظتها في الأغنام. الإبلاغ السريع ضروري لحماية بقية الحيوانات.

diseases.zoonoticNote: FMD is not considered a practical human zoonosis. Normal hygiene and PPE are still important because infected animals contaminate equipment and clothing.
diseases.notifiableNote: WOAH-listed and reportable everywhere with emergency controls. Any suspicion in sheep must be reported immediately because mild cases can spread the virus unnoticed.
diseases.meatNote: FMD in sheep is a reportable emergency; affected flocks are subject to official quarantine and carcass destruction.
diseases.causativeAgent: Foot-and-mouth disease virus, an aphthovirus with multiple serotypes. Sheep can carry and spread virus with only mild lesions, making surveillance difficult.
diseases.affected: Sheep of all ages and other cloven-hoofed animals. Young lambs may die suddenly from heart damage.
symptoms: Fever and mild depression
Blisters or erosions on the mouth, tongue, gums and teats
Drooling and reluctance to eat
Lameness and foot lesions
Reduced milk yield and poor growth
Sudden death in young lambs; some sheep show almost no signs
diseases.diagnosis: Official PCR or antigen testing on vesicular fluid, epithelium or blood is required. Do not collect or move samples without instruction. Trace all contacts, as sheep may show very subtle lesions.
diseases.postMortem: Vesicles and erosions in the mouth, tongue, dental pad, teats and coronary bands; lesions in sheep are often smaller and heal faster than in cattle. Myocardial necrosis can occur in young lambs. Do not open a suspect carcass; FMD is notifiable and samples must be collected through official channels with strict biosecurity.
diseases.treatment: There is no specific antiviral treatment. Supportive care may be provided under official direction, with antibiotics only for secondary infection. Outbreak control commonly includes culling, movement restrictions and vaccination where permitted.
diseases.prevention: Use strain-matched vaccination only under official programmes, maintain strict biosecurity, quarantine introduced animals and follow all movement controls. Report any mouth or foot blisters immediately.

summary.en: A soil-borne bacterial infection that causes sudden death and bloody discharge in sheep. It is a serious zoonosis; carcasses must not be opened.
summary.ku: نەخۆشییەکی باکتریایی خاکە کە مردنی لەناکاو و دەردانی خوێناوی لە مەڕ دروست دەکات. نەخۆشییەکی مەترسیدارە بۆ مرۆڤ؛ نابێت تەرم بکرێتەوە.
summary.ar: عدوى بكتيرية من التربة تسبب موتاً مفاجئاً وإفرازات دموية في الأغنام. وهي مرض حيواني المنشأ خطير؛ يجب عدم فتح الجثث.

diseases.zoonoticNote: Yes, a serious zoonosis. Spores can enter through skin cuts, inhalation or ingestion. Never open a suspicious carcass; contact authorities and seek medical advice after exposure.
diseases.notifiableNote: Emergency reportable in nearly every country. Report sudden deaths with bloody discharge immediately and isolate the area.
diseases.meatNote: Never open or consume carcasses of sheep suspected of anthrax; it is a lethal zoonotic disease.
diseases.causativeAgent: Bacillus anthracis, a spore-forming bacterium. Spores persist in soil for decades and can concentrate in low-lying grazing areas after flooding or soil disturbance.
diseases.affected: Sheep and cattle of all ages, especially grazing animals in endemic regions. People and other mammals are susceptible.
symptoms: Sudden death, often the first sign
Bloodstained discharge from the nose, mouth or anus
High fever and rapid collapse in the short course
Breathing difficulty and colic-like signs
Soft swelling of the head, neck or brisket
Blood may fail to clot after death
diseases.diagnosis: Do not perform a routine necropsy. Report immediately and allow official staff to collect blood or an ear sample for staining, culture or PCR. Rapid laboratory confirmation protects people and other animals.
diseases.postMortem: Suspected anthrax must never be opened. The carcass may show rapid bloating, dark tarry blood from the nose, mouth or anus, and incomplete rigor; blood smears may show encapsulated bacilli. If opened, splenomegaly and haemorrhages may be seen, but this creates a serious human and environmental hazard. Notify the authorities before any handling and do not perform a field necropsy.
diseases.treatment: Early antibiotics under official direction may help in the very early stage. Carcasses must be disposed of by incineration or deep burial with lime according to regulations. Contact with carcasses, blood or contaminated soil requires urgent medical assessment and prophylaxis.
diseases.prevention: Vaccinate sheep in endemic areas according to official schedules. Avoid grazing known contaminated sites, maintain drainage, do not move carcasses and use full PPE for official sampling. Control flies around dead animals.

summary.en: A respiratory disease complex causing cough, fever and breathing difficulty, especially after transport, crowding or mixing. Acute bacterial pneumonia can kill quickly.
summary.ku: نەخۆشییەکی ئاڵۆزی هەناسەدانە کە کۆکە، تا و سەختێی هەناسەدان دروست دەکات، بەتایبەتی دوای گواستنەوە، قەرەباڵغی یان تێکەڵکردن. سیەسۆیلی باکتریایی دەتوانێت بە خێرایی بکوژێت.
summary.ar: مرض تنفسي مركب يسبب السعال والحمى وصعوبة التنفس، خاصة بعد النقل أو الازدحام أو الخلط. الالتهاب الرئوي البكتيري الحاد قد يقتل بسرعة.

diseases.zoonoticNote: The usual sheep respiratory pathogens are not a public-health zoonosis, but some can infect people with close contact. Maintain hygiene.
diseases.notifiableNote: Not usually notifiable as a syndrome, but specific pathogens may require reporting.
diseases.meatNote: Meat from recovered sheep is fit after routine slaughter inspection and completion of antibiotic withdrawal periods.
diseases.causativeAgent: Mannheimia haemolytica, Bibersteinia trehalosi, Pasteurella multocida, Mycoplasma ovipneumoniae and respiratory viruses. Poor ventilation, transport stress, dust, weaning and crowding trigger outbreaks.
diseases.affected: Sheep of all ages. Lambs after transport or weaning, housed flocks and ewes around lambing are most at risk. Acute pasteurellosis can affect healthy-looking young sheep.
symptoms: Cough and nasal discharge
Fast, shallow breathing and flared nostrils
Fever, dullness and reduced appetite
Weight loss and lagging behind the flock
Sudden death in acute pasteurellosis
Reduced growth in surviving lambs
diseases.diagnosis: Assess temperature, breathing rate and lung sounds. In outbreaks, use appropriate nasal or lung samples for bacterial and viral testing. Review housing, stocking density and recent transport or mixing.
diseases.postMortem: Consolidated, dark-red to grey lung tissue, often cranioventral, with frothy or purulent airway exudate; pleurisy and abscesses may be present. Bronchial and mediastinal lymph nodes are enlarged. In maedi-visna or ovine pulmonary adenocarcinoma the lungs are firm and heavy, and tumours may be found. Collect lung and airway samples for bacterial, viral and parasitic testing.
diseases.treatment: Prompt veterinary examination and supportive care are important. Use antibiotics only for likely bacterial pneumonia, following local guidelines and culture where possible. NSAIDs may reduce fever and pain. Separate sick animals and improve ventilation.
diseases.prevention: Ensure good colostrum and lamb nutrition, avoid overcrowding and poor ventilation, reduce transport and mixing stress, and quarantine new sheep. Vaccinate against relevant pathogens where available and review housing with a veterinarian.
